name: Fireworks AI On-Demand deployments (per GPU-second)
region: primary regions plus region-restricted deployments at a 1.5x premium
price_basis: per GPU-hour, 'Pay per GPU second, with no extra charges for start-up times'. H100 80GB $0.134/min = $8.00/h; H200 141GB $0.134/min = $8.00/h; B200 180GB $0.217/min = $13.00/h; B300 288GB $0.250/min = $15.00/h; GB300 $0.334/min = $20.00/h. Fetched 2026-10-03. PRICE CLASS: this is a PUBLISHED LIST PRICE - an asking rate a new customer is quoted, not a realised, discounted or negotiated transaction rate. A real bill is at or below this and typically well below it once commitments, credits and committed-use discounts are applied.
notes:
Fireworks is INFERENCE-SHAPED, and the price reflects it: at $8.00/H100-hour this is the second most expensive on-demand H100 in the slice, above AWS p5's $6.88 and far above Runpod's $3.49, and you get a dedicated deployment with their inference runtime rather than a bare GPU. That is a deliberate trade, not a mistake - compare it to Runpod serverless H100 ($4.79 per worker-hour) or CoreWeave's inference-platform H100 ($6.16, but gated to that platform) and the picture is that Fireworks is priced as a product, not as silicon. Two real details. (1) The published minute and hour columns are internally inconsistent - $0.134 x 60 = $8.04, printed as $8.00 - so treat the hourly figure as a rounded convenience and the per-minute figure as the one that is actually charged. (2) Region-restricted deployments are a stated 1.5x premium, which on H100 is $12.00/hour and would put a data-residency requirement above every hyperscaler in this slice. Fireworks also publishes per-token serverless and per-token training prices on the same page; those are a different unit and are deliberately not recorded as supply. Their per-second billing with no start-up charge is the genuinely useful engineering property here.

 EXPORT CONTROL (2026-10-04, mechanism-level; sources spl-bis-2026-05-d5-guidance, spl-bis-2026-01-advanced-computing-case-by-case): renting capacity does NOT remove the export-control question, it relocates it. Providing remote access to controlled computing capability can constitute a transfer under the EAR, so the provider must screen the end user; and separately, under the 91 FR 1684 licence regime the consignee must run KYC procedures to prevent unauthorized remote access and must manage and limit IaaS access to the hardware - obligations pushed onto the customer, who must be told to implement them. For a customer headquartered or parented in Country Group D:5 or Macau the 742.6(a)(6)(iii)(A) end-user/parent test can bite even when the capacity is consumed in a permitted region. Recorded true because the underlying hardware is controlled and the provider carries the screening duty, not because access to a US region is itself restricted.

 LEAD TIME: null, and correct as null. For a listed on-demand instance type the provisioning delay is effectively zero - capacity is allocated per request - so a week count would be meaningless; the real gate for scarce shapes is either a quota increase or a capacity reservation, not a lead time. Where a published commitment horizon exists it IS recorded: AWS documents that a Capacity Block may be reserved with a start time up to EIGHT WEEKS in the future (source spl-aws-capacity-block-booking-horizon), which is a floor on how far ahead scarce capacity must be committed, not a wait. On-demand and Spot tiers publish no lead time at all; their constraint is availability, and the repo records that as availability=in-stock or a spot/reality note rather than as a fabricated week figure. Probe log in source spl-negative-no-oem-publishes-lead-time.
